monte_carlo_oprisk_capital.text: `advanced_measurement_approach_ama` answers "what AMA capital charge comes out of my own loss history?", while `monte_carlo_oprisk_capital` answers "what capital and expected shortfall result from loss-process parameters I already have?". The AMA function takes raw history (`annual_event_counts` and `loss_amounts`), fits a Poisson frequency and lognormal severity internally, and then runs a Monte Carlo quantile. The Monte Carlo function skips the fitting: you supply `frequency_lambda`, `severity_mu` and `severity_sigma` directly, and it reports expected shortfall alongside OpVaR. Its capital is always OpVaR minus expected loss, whereas `advanced_measurement_approach_ama` has an `expected_loss_covered` switch: true gives OpVaR minus expected loss, false gives the full OpVaR. AMA is also retired for Basel III/IV regulatory capital, so it suits economic-capital work, internal scenario analysis and earlier-timeline jurisdictions.

explain.text: `advanced_measurement_approach_ama` computes an operational risk capital charge under the Advanced Measurement Approach, which Basel III/IV has retired in favour of the standardised measurement approach (`basel_standardised_measurement_sma`). pyvar keeps it for economic-capital work, internal scenario analysis and jurisdictions on earlier timelines. From your `annual_event_counts` and `loss_amounts`, it fits frequency and severity models and runs a Monte Carlo simulation to get OpVaR and expected loss. If `expected_loss_covered` is true, capital is OpVaR minus EL (floored at zero); otherwise it is the full OpVaR.

when.text:
`advanced_measurement_approach_ama` (Advanced Measurement Approach) fits a fairly narrow set of situations:

- You need an economic-capital or internal scenario-analysis view of operational risk built from your own loss history (`annual_event_counts` and `loss_amounts`).
- You work in a jurisdiction still on earlier timelines, where the AMA and its LDA internal model remain relevant.
- You want to see how capital changes depending on whether expected loss is demonstrably covered in provisions, using `expected_loss_covered`.
- Don't use it for Basel III/IV regulatory capital. The AMA is retired there and superseded by `basel_standardised_measurement_sma`.

If you only want the end-to-end Loss Distribution Approach capital estimate, `loss_distribution_approach_lda` is listed as doing that.
